title: Pāśupata Sūtra

attribution.tradition: Taught by the Lord (Bhagavat, Paśupati) who took a brahmin's body at Kāyāvataraṇa and taught Kuśika at Ujjayinī (Kauṇḍinya); later sources call the speaker Nakulīśa / Lakulīśa (Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha ch. 6).
attribution.scholarly: An anonymous sūtra text preserved only with Kauṇḍinya's commentary; composed before Kauṇḍinya. Its attribution to a historical Lakulīśa is the tradition's.

tradition.text: revealed by Śiva incarnate as Lakulīśa

scholarly.text: before Kauṇḍinya (4th–6th c.); often placed in the early centuries CE

structure.description: five adhyāyas of short sūtras - 44, 27, 26, 24 and 47 in the Sagar-based numbering (168 in all, with a lacuna at 5.29); 167 in the Sastri-based numbering. Each adhyāya closes with one of the five brahma-mantras (Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna).

summary: The root text of the Pāśupatas. Adhyāya 1 prescribes the first-stage observance in the temple (ash-bathing thrice daily, lying in ash, wearing the used garland, the six-limbed offering of laughter, song, dance, the ḍuṇḍuṅkāra sound, prostration and muttering) and lists the powers that arise; adhyāyas 2-4 teach worship of Rudra alone, courting dishonour by feigned madness and the transfer of merit and sin, and non-return; adhyāya 5 teaches the solitary yogin in empty houses, caves and cremation grounds, meditation on Oṃ in the heart, constant remembrance of Rudra and the end of suffering by the Lord's grace.

editions.name: R. Ananthakrishna Sastri, Pāśupata Sūtras with Pañcārthabhāṣya of Kauṇḍinya, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series 143 (1940)
K. Sagar ed., Varanasi 1987; GRETIL e-text input by R. Grünendahl

title: Pañcārthabhāṣya
alt_titles: Kauṇḍinya's commentary on the Pāśupata Sūtra

attribution.tradition: 'Composed by the revered Kauṇḍinya' (colophon of each adhyāya).
attribution.scholarly: Kauṇḍinya, c. 4th–6th c. CE. Some scholars have identified him with the Pāśupata tīrthakara Rāśīkara, whose 'bhāṣya' the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha cites; the identification is uncertain.

structure.description: prose commentary on every sūtra, in five adhyāyas; opens with a verse naming Kauṇḍinya

summary: Kauṇḍinya's commentary reads the Pāśupata Sūtra as teaching five categories (effect, cause, union, rule, end of suffering), defines the Lord, the soul and the bonds, the three means of knowledge, the yamas and niyamas, the six 'doors' of feigned behaviour and the exchange of merit and sin, and correlates the sūtras with a five-stage path (residence, livelihood, strength, action, purification and gain for each stage). It holds that the end of suffering comes by the Lord's grace and that the Lord does not depend on karma.

editions.name: R. Ananthakrishna Sastri ed., TSS 143 (1940)
GRETIL e-text input by O. Hellwig (based on Sastri 1940)
editions.licence: GRETIL e-text: reference use; copyright as for the source edition

notes: Known from a single rediscovered manuscript published in 1940.

title: Gaṇakārikā

attribution.tradition: The Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha (ch. 6) quotes its verses as the words of Haradattācārya.
attribution.scholarly: Dalal's 1920 edition ascribes the verses to Bhāsarvajña, author of the Ratnaṭīkā; others ascribe the verses to Haradatta and only the commentary to Bhāsarvajña.

scholarly.text: c. 10th c. or earlier (depends on authorship)

summary: Eight verses naming the nine groups (gaṇa) of the Pāśupata system: eight pentads - gains (lābha), impurities (mala), means (upāya), places (deśa), stages (avasthā), purifications (viśuddhi), factors of initiation (dīkṣākārin) and strengths (bala) - and one triad of livelihoods (vṛtti). The teacher is he who knows these nine groups and consecrates the disciple.

editions.name: C. D. Dalal ed., Gaṇakārikā with Ratnaṭīkā, Gaekwad's Oriental Series 15, Baroda 1920 (with appendices)
Muktabodha e-text M00508

title: Ratnaṭīkā

attribution.tradition: Ascribed to Bhāsarvajña in Dalal's edition.
attribution.scholarly: Generally accepted as Bhāsarvajña's (c. 10th c.); the author cites his own teacher.

summary: Prose commentary on the Gaṇakārikā. It explains each of the nine groups; maps the five stages to places (teacher, people, cave, cremation ground, Rudra) and livelihoods; describes the daily observance (ash-baths at the three junctures, the six-limbed offering in the temple, circumambulation, salutation of the tīrthakaras from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara); defines the six 'doors'; and distinguishes a true teacher from a pseudo-teacher (ācāryābhāsa).

editions.name: C. D. Dalal ed., GOS 15, Baroda 1920
Muktabodha e-text M00508

title: Kāravaṇa-māhātmya

attribution.tradition: Presents itself as part of the Vāyu Purāṇa (colophon of ch. 1, 'Śivaprasūtisarga') and of the Śiva Purāṇa ('Lakulīśa-māhātmya', later colophons); a dialogue of Śiva and Pārvatī.
attribution.scholarly: A local glorification of Kāyāvarohaṇa (Karvan, Gujarat) of unknown date, printed as an appendix to Dalal's Gaṇakārikā (1920).

summary: Śiva tells Pārvatī of his descent between the Dvāpara and Kali ages: he is born at Ulkāgrāma to the brahmin Viśvarūpa of Atri's line and his wife Sudarśanā; the infant secretly performs the fire-offering; he dies at seven months, is laid in the sacred pool, and Śiva enters the body, which is found alive; as Lakulīśa he comes to Kāyāvarohaṇa in the Bhṛgu region and merges into the Brahmeśvara liṅga. The tīrtha bears a different name in each age.

editions.name: appendix IV to C. D. Dalal ed., Gaṇakārikā, GOS 15 (1920); Muktabodha M00508

title: Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha

attribution.scholarly: A 14th-c. Advaita doxography by a Mādhava whose identity is disputed.

structure.description: sixteen chapters presenting sixteen systems in ascending order, ending with Śaṅkara's Advaita; ch. 6 on the Nakulīśa-Pāśupatas

summary: Its sixth chapter presents the Pāśupata system in its own terms: the five categories with their subdivisions, the twofold end of suffering (cessation, and the Lord's powers of knowing and acting), the vows and six 'doors', the Gaṇakārikā's pentads (quoted as Haradatta's), the Pāśupata claims of distinctiveness, and a defence of the Lord's independence from karma.

editions.name: ch. 6 reprinted as appendix II to Dalal, GOS 15 (1920); Muktabodha M00508

title: Rāśīkara-bhāṣya

attribution.tradition: Named in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha (ch. 6) as the place where the five categories are set out in detail with the means of knowledge.
attribution.scholarly: Possibly identical with Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya (if Kauṇḍinya = Rāśīkara); otherwise lost.

summary: A Pāśupata commentary known only by name from the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha.

title: Ādarśa (Pāśupata work)

attribution.tradition: The Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha (ch. 6) cites 'the author of the Ādarśa and other tīrthakaras' for the definitions of the Lord's attributes.
attribution.scholarly: Otherwise unknown; presumably lost.

summary: A lost Pāśupata treatise known only from a mention in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha.

title: Pañcārthabhāṣyadīpikā

attribution.tradition: Named in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha (ch. 6) as giving the detailed exposition of the effect (vidyā, kalā, paśu).
attribution.scholarly: Probably a sub-commentary on the Pañcārthabhāṣya; not known to survive.

summary: A Pāśupata work, apparently a gloss on Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya, known only by name.

title: Niśvāsamukha

attribution.tradition: revealed Śaiva scripture (the introductory book of the Niśvāsa corpus)
attribution.scholarly: Introductory book of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, later than the Mūlasūtra (c. 450–550 CE); critical edition by N. Kafle (2020).

summary: Surveys Śaiva revelation as five streams: the worldly (laukika), the Vedic (vaidika), the spiritual (ādhyātmika: Sāṃkhya and Yoga), the Atimārga and the Mantra path. Its account of the Atimārga describes the Pāśupata observance 'beyond the āśramas' and the Lākula observance 'beyond the world' with skull and khaṭvāṅga.

editions.name: N. Kafle, The Niśvāsamukha, the introductory book of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (Pondicherry: IFP/EFEO, 2020)

notes: Not available in this run's local corpus; chapter-level references are from memory (low confidence).

title: Āgamaprāmāṇya

attribution.scholarly: Yāmuna, c. 10th–11th c.

summary: Yāmuna's defence of the Vedic authority of the Pāñcarātra. Contrasting it with the 'Māheśvara' tantras, he names four Śaiva groups - Kāpālikas, Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas and Śaivas - and reports the Kāpālika six insignia and yoni-meditation, the Kālāmukha skull and corpse-ash practices, the Pāśupata five categories, and the claim that initiation makes one a brahmin at once; he judges all of them outside the Veda.

J. A. B. van Buitenen, Yāmuna's Āgama Prāmāṇyam (1971)

title: Mattavilāsa-prahasana

attribution.scholarly: the Pallava king Mahendravarman I, early 7th c.

summary: A one-act farce set in Kāñcī. The drunken Kāpālika Satyasoma and his companion Devasomā lose their skull begging-bowl, accuse the Buddhist monk Nāgasena, appeal to the Pāśupata Babhrukalpa, and recover the bowl from a madman who took it from a dog. It satirises Kāpālika, Buddhist and Pāśupata ascetics.

title: Mālatīmādhava

attribution.scholarly: Bhavabhūti, early 8th c.

summary: A ten-act drama. The Kāpālika Aghoraghaṇṭa, come from Śrīparvata, and his female disciple Kapālakuṇḍalā plan to offer the heroine Mālatī to the goddess Karālā (Cāmuṇḍā) at the great cremation ground; the hero Mādhava kills Aghoraghaṇṭa (act 5) and Kapālakuṇḍalā seeks revenge. Kapālakuṇḍalā enters flying and speaks of the channels, the heart-lotus and the Lord of the Śaktis.

title: Prabodhacandrodaya

attribution.scholarly: Kṛṣṇamiśra, at the Candella court (Kīrtivarman), late 11th c.

summary: An allegorical drama in six acts in which Viveka defeats Mahāmoha. In act 3 a Kāpālika appears beside a Digambara Jain and a Buddhist monk, boasts of worshipping Mahābhairava with human offerings and of his powers, and wins both over with liquor and his female companion; his doctrine is called Somasiddhānta.
notes: Not found in this run's local corpus; act-level references only.

title: Yaśastilaka

attribution.scholarly: the Digambara Somadeva Sūri, completed 959 CE

summary: A Jain prose-and-verse romance. Its frame story turns on a king urged to offer pairs of living beings to a goddess, and it contains polemical accounts of rival religious practice, including Kaula and Kāpālika ways (details to be checked).
notes: Low confidence on the specific Kāpālika passages; not checked against the text in this run.

title: Gāthāsaptaśatī

attribution.tradition: compiled by the Sātavāhana king Hāla
attribution.scholarly: anthology compiled in the early centuries CE with later additions; date uncertain

scholarly.text: early centuries CE onward (layers of uncertain date)

summary: An anthology of seven hundred Prakrit verses; verse 408 (Weber) pictures a newly initiated female Kāpālika smearing herself with the ash of her lover's pyre - often cited as the earliest literary mention of Kāpālikas.

editions.name: A. Weber, Das Saptaçatakam des Hâla (1881); GRETIL e-text

title: Śaṅkaradigvijaya

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Vidyāraṇya disputed; dates proposed from the 14th to the 18th c.

summary: A verse hagiography of Śaṅkara. It narrates his encounters with Kāpālikas - Ugrabhairava, who asked for his head as an offering at Śrīśaila and was killed by Padmapāda possessed by Narasiṃha, and Krakaca at Ujjayinī - as victories of Advaita (hagiography by opponents of the Kāpālikas).

title: Harṣacarita

attribution.scholarly: Bāṇa, court poet of Harṣavardhana, 7th c.

summary: Bāṇa's account of Harṣa and his ancestors. Chapter 3 tells how king Puṣpabhūti, a devout Māheśvara, honoured Bhairavācārya, a great Śaiva from the south with thousands of disciples, and assisted him in a night rite in the great cremation ground.

editions.name: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) text

notes: Listed under the Kāpālikas because scholarship discusses Bhairavācārya among portraits of skull-and-cremation-ground Śaiva ascetics; the text itself calls him a great Śaiva (mahāśaiva), not a Kāpālika.

title: Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Records of the Western Regions of the Great Tang)

attribution.scholarly: 646 CE

summary: Xuanzang's record of his journey; it notes 'ash-smearing' ascetics (usually taken as Pāśupatas) at many Indian sites and, in its general account of India, ascetics who wear skulls.

title: Tarkarahasyadīpikā

attribution.scholarly: the Tapāgaccha monk Guṇaratna, c. 1400–1410

summary: Guṇaratna's commentary on Haribhadra's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya. On the Naiyāyikas it describes them as Śaiva ascetics (staff, loincloth, matted hair, ash, sacred thread), lists the eighteen avatāras/tīrtheśas of their god from Nakulīśa to Vidyāguru, divides the ascetics into four kinds - Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Mahāvratadharas and Kālamukhas - and says Naiyāyikas are called Śaivas and Vaiśeṣikas Pāśupatas.

editions.name: excerpt as appendix II (headed 'from the Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya of Haribhadra') to Dalal, GOS 15 (1920); Muktabodha M00508

notes: The appendix heading names Haribhadra; the prose is taken here to be Guṇaratna's commentary (moderate confidence).

title: Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (Rājaśekhara Sūri)

attribution.scholarly: the Jain Rājaśekhara Sūri, 1348 CE

summary: A verse doxography. Its 'Śaiva' (= Yauga/Naiyāyika) section describes the ascetics' dress and greeting, lists the eighteen avatāras of Śaṅkara worshipped as tīrtheśas (Nakulīśa, Kauśika, Gārgya, Maitrya, Kauruṣa, Īśāna, Pāragārgya, Kapilāṇḍa, Manuṣyaka, Aparakuśika, Atri, Piṅgalākṣa, Puṣpaka, Bṛhadācārya, Agasti, Santāna, Rāśīkara, Vidyāguru), names Akṣapāda as their guru, and says bharaṭas of any varṇa serve as priests.

editions.name: excerpt as appendix III to Dalal, GOS 15 (1920); Muktabodha M00508

title: Kiraṇavṛtti
alt_titles: Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's commentary on the Kiraṇatantra

attribution.scholarly: Rāmakaṇṭha, Kashmir, c. 950–1000

summary: Rāmakaṇṭha's Siddhānta commentary on the Kiraṇatantra; among much else it defines liberation as the manifestation of the soul's own Śiva-nature and rejects the rival accounts of transfer, possession and production of the Lord's qualities.

title: Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad

attribution.scholarly: a Śaiva Upaniṣad; date uncertain

summary: Rudra declares himself to be everything; the gods praise him; the text ends (section 5 in the edition used) with the ash vow called pāśupata - 'fire is ash, wind is ash, water is ash, earth is ash, sky is ash' - for release from the bond of the paśu, and contains a verbal parallel to Pāśupata Sūtra 5.35-38.

title: Mathurā pillar inscription of Candragupta II (Gupta year 61)

attribution.tradition: record of the Pāśupata teacher Uditācārya
attribution.scholarly: dated Gupta year 61 = 380 CE; published by D. R. Bhandarkar (Epigraphia Indica)

summary: Records that Uditācārya, tenth in succession from Kuśika, installed in a teachers' shrine two liṅgas named after his teachers (Kapileśvara and Upamiteśvara). The earliest dated evidence for the Pāśupata lineage of Kuśika and the basis of the scholarly dating of Lakulīśa.

title: Ekaliṅgajī (Lakulīśa temple) inscription of 971 CE

attribution.scholarly: inscription of VS 1028 (971 CE) in the Lakulīśa ('Nāth') temple at Ekaliṅgajī near Udaipur

summary: A Pāśupata record from Mewar that refers to Lakulīśa's descent in the region of Bhṛgukaccha and to Pāśupata ascetics of the Kuśika line (details to be checked).

title: Prabhāsa-pāṭan (Bhadrakālī) inscription of 1169 CE

attribution.scholarly: Valabhī year 850 = 1169 CE, reign of the Caulukya Kumārapāla

summary: Eulogy of the Pāśupata ācārya Bhāva Bṛhaspati, who came to Somanātha and, under Kumārapāla, directed the restoration of the temple.

title: Cintra praśasti (1287 CE)

attribution.scholarly: a Somanātha eulogy of 1287 CE (reign of the Vāghela Sāraṅgadeva), the stone now at Sintra (Portugal)

summary: Eulogy of the Pāśupata ascetic Tripurāntaka and his foundations at Somanātha; it recounts Lakulīśa's incarnation and his four disciples as founders of four lines (details to be checked).

title: Balligāve (Belagāmi) inscriptions of the Kālāmukha Kōḍiya-maṭha

attribution.scholarly: inscriptions of the 11th–13th c. at Balligāve (Shikarpur taluk, Shimoga district), published in Epigraphia Carnatica

summary: Records of the Kōḍiya-maṭha attached to the Dakṣiṇa-Kedāreśvara temple at Balligāve, seat of the Śakti-pariṣad of the Kālāmukhas: grants, lineages of pontiffs, and praise of their learning and of the maṭha's feeding, teaching and healing.
